title: The quantum endgame isn't cleaner qubits, it's who can mass-produce on a phone-chip line
dek: The endgame of quantum computing isn't whose qubits are cleaner, it's who can mass-produce on existing semiconductor lines; silicon spin qubits reuse TSMC's lithography, while trapped ions are stuck at a hundred thousand laser beams and superconductors at warehouse-scale refrigerators.
why: The exclusive value is in the back half: the CNOT error rate from the HRL paper, AI auto-tuning, FFP's astonishing scores; the first half's explanation of principles leans popular-science, and veterans can fast-forward.
who: Investors watching quantum computing's route selection, semiconductor process engineers, and security practitioners who want to calibrate the quantum-cryptobreaking timeline.
skip: Listeners already familiar with superconducting and trapped-ion principles can skip 57:56 to 1:28:00.

points.h: Trapped ions and superconductors must invent a miracle first; silicon doesn't
points.body: To build a hundred-thousand-qubit trapped-ion machine, you first have to invent the optical miracle of a hundred thousand laser beams; a million superconducting qubits require a warehouse-sized cryostat; a million spin qubits need only a standard 300mm silicon wafer, run through the same lithography equipment TSMC, ASML and Intel use to make phone processors. Krishna uses this to set the tone for the whole episode: the key to the quantum race isn't single-qubit fidelity, it's whether a path to scale already exists inside the industrial system.

points.h: Quantum computing has stopped comparing principles and started comparing engineering
points.body: In 2000 DiVincenzo proposed five criteria, with the aim of ruling out liquid NMR quantum computing. In this episode FFP proposes three criteria of its own: qubit quality, control, and scalability and economics. The rest of the episode scores four routes — superconducting, trapped ion, neutral atom, silicon spin — item by item. Simply laying out the evaluation framework tells you: quantum computing has entered the engineering-competition phase, and you can't just talk about principles.

points.h: Superconducting isn't a technology failure, it's an engineering one that won't fit
points.body: Estimates suggest a thousand logical qubits require ten million transmon physical qubits. The number of control lines is limited by the dilution refrigerator's cooling capacity, frequencies are crowded, and helium-3 supply becomes a new resource constraint. FFP gives superconducting just 1/10 on scalability and economics, for a total of 11/30. This is the first time in the episode that "technically strong" and "engineering-infeasible" are scored separately; a warehouse-sized cryostat means even a data center may not be able to house it.

points.h: Trapped ions win on coherence time and lose on gate speed
points.body: Trapped-ion coherence times run as long as ten hours, but gate operations depend on phonons and are limited by the Paul trap's oscillation frequency, making them roughly a thousand times slower than superconducting. The result is counterintuitive: even if trapped ions could scale to cryptobreaking size, breaking 2048-bit RSA would take about a year, whereas superconducting would take about eight hours. Long coherence time does not equal more done per unit time; for practical computation, slow gate times are a throughput catastrophe overall.

points.h: The quantum threat is neither tomorrow nor forever
points.body: A March 2026 paper from Harvard, Caltech and Qera says ten thousand qubits might break internet encryption, but in practice it would take years; even with a hundred thousand physical qubits, breaking RSA under the mathematically optimal assumption takes about three months. This number strikes at both extreme narratives at once: the quantum threat is not tomorrow, but it is by no means forever distant. To achieve "breakable within months" requires qubit count, gate speed and error correction to all hit the mark simultaneously.

points.h: Quantum companies live and die by government contracts
points.body: HRL lost key project funding in early 2026 and laid off 376 people. Government funding shifted from basic research toward applied research demanding rapid commercialization; IBM and Intel got support through the CHIPS Act, and eventually IBM acquired HRL. Krishna calls this the arrival of the quantum-computing MVP: quantum companies live or die by government contracts, and being acquired isn't failure — it's letting the technology enter an industrial system with manufacturing capability.

points.h: A million qubits can't be tuned by hand; it has to go to image recognition
points.body: Automated tuning becomes the key to scaling: a 2023 paper had only six electron spins that could be tuned by hand, and hand-tuning a million qubits would take a human lifetime. Tuning is essentially image recognition — when you sweep voltage, tunneling events show up as fringes, and Krishna's team uses DETR, combining ResNet and a Transformer, to automatically recognize the fringes and generate parameters. This is also the hidden precondition for why silicon spin can reuse semiconductor lines: no matter how many qubits there are, software can align them automatically.

points.h: Silicon may not be first to be made, but it will be the last to win
points.body: FFP's final scores: silicon spin gets 10/10 on qubit quality, 10/10 on control (provided the isotope enrichment and valley-state problems are solved), 10000/10 on scalability and economics, for a total of 10020/30; by contrast neutral atoms score negative 3000. Krishna concedes silicon may not be the first route to fault tolerance, but once it gets there, being cheap and easy to manufacture will make it the eventual standard, just as the transistor replaced the vacuum tube.
